      "text": "[Document context]\nTitle: scheduled scale profiles + fairness-aware fleet scaler\nSource: EnterpriseRAG/github\nPath: /knowledge/company/sources/github/pr-42812-scheduled-profiles-and-fairness-scaler.json\nConnector: github\nWorkspace: pr-42812-scheduled-profiles-and-fairness-scaler.json\n\nscale profile concept plus a fairness - aware scaler that reserves and enforces tenant headroom percentages during scheduled windows. what this change does ( high level ) : adds a scaleprofile crd - like config for dedicated ( stored in control plane tenant config ), implements time - based scale profiles in the fleet autoscaler, and augments the scheduler to compute and enforce tenant headroom fractions. the scaler now supports : 1 ) scheduled up / down adjustments ( scale profiles ), 2 ) tenant - level soft guarantees ( headroom _ pct ) that allocate reserved burst capacity, and 3 ) fairness rebalancing to avoid long - term capacity starvation.",

document.content:
{
  "repo": "redwood",
  "pr_number": "42812",
  "title": "scheduled scale profiles + fairness-aware fleet scaler",
  "author": "Asha Patel",
  "created_at": "2026-02-15",
  "updated_at": "2026-02-22",
  "merged_at": "2026-02-22",
  "state": "merged",
  "base_branch": "main",
  "head_branch": "feature/fleet-scheduler-fairness-scaler",
  "description": "Motivation: customers with mixed workloads asked for predictable dedicated capacity behavior during known peak windows (daily batch jobs, nightly ingest, marketing campaigns) while preserving per-tenant fairness and soft throughput guarantees. This PR introduces a scheduler-based scale profile concept plus a fairness-aware scaler that reserves and enforces tenant headroom percentages during scheduled windows.\n\nWhat this change does (high level): adds a ScaleProfile CRD-like config for Dedicated (stored in control plane tenant config), implements time-based scale profiles in the fleet autoscaler, and augments the scheduler to compute and enforce tenant headroom fractions. The scaler now supports: 1) scheduled up/down adjustments (scale profiles), 2) tenant-level soft guarantees (headroom_pct) that allocate reserved burst capacity, and 3) fairness rebalancing to avoid long-term capacity starvation.\n\nKey behaviors and guarantees: - Scheduled profiles are applied with configurable pre-warm lead time (default 10m) to allow provisioning GPU pools before the window. - Headroom_pct is a soft-guarantee: the allocator attempts to preserve the specified percent of spare capacity per tenant but will yield if global capacity becomes constrained. - Fairness rebalancer runs every 60s and tries to minimize sustained deviation from baseline allocations; it is low-priority and will not preempt active requests.\n\nBackward compatibility and migration: existing Dedicated configs continue to work. New config fields have defaults that preserve current autoscaler behavior (headroom_pct=0, no scheduled profiles). Migration plan: control plane database migration adds the scale_profiles table and backfills empty value; the fleet-controller tolerates both old and new records for 48 hours post-deploy.\n\nTesting and telemetry: end-to-end integration tests added for scheduled windows, pre-warm behavior, and fairness under contention. New metrics: fleet_scale_profile_applied{profile,name}, tenant_headroom_utilization_pct, fairness_rebalance_actions_total. Dashboards updated: Dedicated -> Capacity -> Scheduled Profiles; an alert (SLO) for pre-warm misses added (dedicated.prewarm.miss > 0 for 5m).\n\nRollout plan: staged rollout: control plane first (feature flag), then fleet-controller + autoscaler; feature flag can be turned off to restore legacy behavior. We will enable for internal QA for 48h, then enable for a subset of enterprise tenants, and finally full rollout.\n\nChecklist:\n- [x] Autoscaler algorithm implemented and unit-tested\n- [x] Scheduler integration + pre-warm hook\n- [x] API surface for tenant scale profiles + schema migration\n- [x] End-to-end tests for scheduled up/down and fairness rebalancing\n- [x] Telemetry, dashboards, and alerting\n- [x] Migration and rollback plan documented\n\nRelated items: Linear ENG-7321, ENG-7389; RFC: /docs/rfcs/fleet-schedule-profiles.md\n\nNotes: there are a few known follow-ups tracked in ENG-7420 (deterministic allocation ordering) and ENG-7471 (adaptive pre-warm based on historical cold-starts).",
  "commits": [
    "a1f3e9b  Implemented ScaleProfile config and DB migration",
    "d4b2c88  Fleet scaler: scheduled window handling + pre-warm logic",
    "9f7a21c  Introduced tenant headroom accounting and fairness rebalancer",
    "be3d110  Expose new metrics and update dashboards",
    "5c8a44d  Add e2e tests and integration harness updates",
    "c2f90e7  Docs: RFC link, API examples and migration notes"
  ],
  "files_changed_count": "21",
  "additions": "1387",
  "deletions": "492",
  "files_changed": [
    "fleet/controller/scale_profile.go  (new) - core scheduler for applying profiles and pre-warm hooks",
    "fleet/controller/allocator.go  - add headroom accounting hooks and fairness rebalance loop",
    "controlplane/api/tenant_config.proto  - add ScaleProfile message and headroom_pct field",
    "db/migrations/2026_02_15_add_scale_profiles.sql  (new) - migration to add scale_profiles table",
    "telemetry/metrics_registry.go  - register tenant_headroom_utilization_pct, fairness_rebalance_actions_total",
    "ui/dashboards/dedicated_profiles.json  - dashboard for scheduled profiles and pre-warm telemetry",
    "integration/tests/scheduled_profile_test.go  - e2e test exercising pre-warm and scheduled scale-up",
    "docs/rfcs/fleet-schedule-profiles.md  - design doc and API examples",
    "api/client/dedicated.go  - client helpers to read/write scale profiles",
    "helm/values.yaml  - feature flag toggle for scale_profiles (default: false)",
    "Makefile and CI pipeline updates  - add e2e job guard for feature flagged runs"
  ],
  "reviewers": [
    "Marco Rivera",
    "Lina Chen",
    "Priya Gupta"
  ],
  "labels": [
    "dedicated",
    "autoscaling",
    "runtime",
    "telemetry",
    "perf",
    "feature"
  ],
  "linked_linear": [
    "ENG-7321",
    "ENG-7389",
    "ENG-7420"
  ],
  "ci_status": "pass",
  "ci_checks": [
    "unit: pass (go test ./... 112s)",
    "integration: pass (e2e with feature flag enabled)",
    "lint: pass (golangci-lint)",
    "helm: pass",
    "deploy-preview: pass (staged control plane)"
  ],
  "review_comments": [
    "Marco Rivera (requested changes): The pre-warm lead time default of 10m seems conservative for small clusters; can we make it adaptive or expose cluster-level override?",
    "Asha Patel (reply): Added cluster_override_ms config and plan to follow up with ENG-7471 for adaptive pre-warm based on historical cold-starts. Kept default 10m to be safe for customers we've seen miss capacity in tests.",
    "Lina Chen (comment): DB migration looks sound but please ensure the migration is idempotent across control plane replicas.",
    "Asha Patel (reply): Verified idempotency; migration uses IF NOT EXISTS and a lightweight backfill job with a lock. Added unit tests for migration run twice.",
    "Priya Gupta (approved): Verified e2e test cases for fairness under contention. Metrics are meaningful and dashboards look good. Approving for merge after CI passes."
  ],
  "merge_method": "squash",
  "merge_commit_summary": "squash: add scheduled scale profiles and fairness-aware fleet scaler; metrics, migration, and e2e tests",
  "release_notes": "Added scheduled scale profiles for Dedicated fleets and a fairness-aware fleet autoscaler. Operators can define time-based scale profiles to pre-warm capacity and set tenant headroom_pct to preserve burst capacity for important tenants. Metrics and dashboards added for observability. Feature is behind a control-plane feature flag and will be opt-in during rollout.",
  "breaking_change": "false",
  "summary": "Adds scheduled scaling profiles and a fairness-enabled autoscaler to improve predictability for scheduled workload peaks while preventing long-term tenant starvation. Includes API, migration, metrics, tests, and rollout plan.",
  "title_field_name": "title",
  "content_field_names": [
    "description",
    "review_comments",
    "release_notes",
    "summary"
  ],

}

{
  "document": {
    "id": "dsid_a3fdfc45905f46f3988ad13f55ecce93",
    "path": "/knowledge/company/sources/linear/engineering/ENG-428317-conditional-multitenant-ratelimiter-priority-skew.json",
    "title": "Conditional multitenant rate limiter priority skew causing transient under-enforcement",
    "source": "EnterpriseRAG/linear",
    "content": "{\n  \"key\": \"ENG-428317\",\n  \"team\": \"engineering\",\n  \"title\": \"Conditional multitenant rate limiter priority skew causing transient under-enforcement\",\n  \"status\": \"In Progress\",\n  \"priority\": \"P1\",\n  \"created_at\": \"2026-03-12\",\n  \"updated_at\": \"2026-03-14\",\n  \"creator\": \"Lina Chen\",\n  \"assignee\": \"Marco Ruiz\",\n  \"project\": \"RateEngine 2.0 - correctness\",\n  \"cycle\": \"2026-Q1-Cycle 5\",\n  \"estimate\": \"5\",\n  \"due_date\": \"2026-03-21\",\n  \"labels\": [\n    \"billing\",\n    \"rate-limiter\",\n    \"investigation\",\n    \"high-impact\"\n  ],\n  \"description\": \"Intermittent cases where per-key priority overrides combined with per-org and per-route policies result in transient under-enforcement (requests allowed when they should be throttled). Observed as short windows of elevated usage for a small set of tenants after shard reassignment and policy hot-reload. This ticket captures investigation, repro, short-term mitigation, and a long-term fix plan.\",\n  \"reproduction_steps\": [\n    \"1) Create two tenants T1 and T2 sharing a shard (sticky-shard assignment enabled).\",\n    \"2) Configure per-org policy: default priority = low, per-route quota = 1000/min.\",\n    \"3) Configure per-key override for a service key K1 belonging to T1: priority = high, burst credits = +200.\",\n    \"4) Start a steady stream of requests from T1 at near-quota rate; verify enforcement hitting quota windows.\",\n    \"5) Trigger a shard reassignment for one edge node (simulate instance bounce or maintenance) while simultaneously applying a policy hot-reload that changes route fallback behavior.\",\n    \"6) Observe a ~10-30s window where requests for K1 are allowed beyond quota; metrics show credits attributed to the wrong in-memory bucket and enforcement checks returning allow from fast-path cache.\",\n    \"7) Collect tracer spans and edge logs for the window; reproduce locally using the shard-reassignment harness and time-accelerated policy reloads.\"\n  ],\n  \"impact\": \"Transient over-allow for small number of tenants leading to underbilling and potential customer perception issues; visible as short-lived bursts up to ~2x expected throughput for affected keys. Affects hosted and dedicated clusters during rolling updates or instance restarts.\",\n  \"customer_impact\": \"medium\",\n  \"logs_snapshot\": [\n    \"edge: allow decision fastpath: key=K1 shard=sh-23 cache_hit=true priority=high quota_window_id=2026-03-12T10:04:00Z\",\n    \"shard-reassign: lease=renewal failover->sh-27 old_owner=sh-23 new_owner=sh-27\",\n    \"policy-hot-reload: version=v2026-03-12-1 route-fallback=enabled\",\n    \"meter-commit: credits_applied target_bucket=org:T2:key:Kx unexpected=true amount=200\"\n  ],\n  \"hypothesis\": \"A race between sticky-shard mapping update and policy hot-reload causes fast-path cache entries (priority and credit pointers) to be re-keyed incorrectly. Per-key overrides store a pointer to a tenant-scoped credit bucket; during reassignment we are dereferencing a stale pointer and applying credits to the wrong tenant's bucket. Enforcement uses the fast-path decision if cache present, so the wrong credits cause an allow where a deny should occur.\",\n  \"experiment_results\": \"Replayed the sequence in staging using the shard-reassign harness. With no policy reload the issue did not occur. When timed policy reload coincided with reassignment, we reproduced the over-allow consistently. Enabling stronger pointer validation (temporary patch) eliminated the over-allows in the harness.\",\n  \"root_cause\": \"Sticky-shard pointer (in-memory bucket reference) is validated only by shard id but not by tenant id during fast-path credit application. Policy hot-reload mutates the route/priority indices while a shard transfer copies pointers; combined these can produce a transient pointer that points at an unrelated tenant's bucket. Enforcement fast-path accepts the cache without full tenant-level validation.\",\n  \"mitigations\": \"Short-term patch deployed to staging: on fast-path cache hit, perform tenant-id validation on the cached credit pointer before applying credits. Also increased grace period on shard handoff to reduce overlap. Rolled patch to canary edge fleet.\",\n  \"rollout_plan\": \"1) Canary for 2 hours on low-traffic region with added telemetry (done). 2) Gradual ramp to 30% of traffic with continued trace sampling for next 24 hours. 3) Full rollout after 48 hours if no regressions. 4) Follow with a database reconciliation backfill job to detect credits misapplied in last 7 days and create accounting fixes if needed.\",\n  \"long_term_fix\": \"Refactor in-memory credit pointer representation to be immutable and namespaced by tenant+shard+route. Replace pointer dereference fast-path with a lightweight validation token check (versioned binder). Add unit and property tests for concurrent shard handoff + policy reload scenarios.\",\n  \"regression_test_plan\": \"Add deterministic concurrency tests to runtime-policy-simulator: combinations of shard reassignment, policy hot-reload, per-key overrides, and burst credit application. Add e2e test in CI harness that exercises rolling updates with randomized interleavings. Add a smoke check after canary verifying no over-allow traces in last 10 minutes.\",\n  \"dependencies\": [\n    \"ENG-430001 (shard-handoff-stabilization)\",\n    \"ENG-429112 (policy-hot-reload-atomicity)\",\n    \"ENG-421007 (prefetch-credit-tombstone-investigation)\"\n  ],\n  \"links\": [\n    \"https://confluence.redwood/inference/rateengine-2.0/priority-pointer-design\",\n    \"https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving/pull/8523 (staging short-term patch)\",\n    \"https://grafana.redwood/board/edge-allow-spikes?from=now-1d&org=tenant\",\n    \"s3://redwood-logs/2026-03-12/shard-hand-off-traces.tar.gz\"\n  ],\n  \"notes\": [\n    \"PM (Aisha Kapoor): prioritize mitigation; billing reconciliation may be needed if misapplied credits persist beyond 24h.\",\n    \"Security (Rajiv Patel): no PII involved in pointers but ensure tracing does not expose tenant ids in public dashboards.\",\n    \"Observation: reproduces more reliably when policy reload contains route fallback toggles rather than pure priority edits.\"\n  ],\n  \"release\": \"rateengine-2.0.3\",\n  \"security_review_required\": \"false\",\n  \"title_field_name\": \"title\",\n  \"content_field_names\": [\n    \"description\",\n    \"impact\",\n    \"reproduction_steps\",\n    \"logs_snapshot\",\n    \"hypothesis\",\n    \"experiment_results\",\n    \"root_cause\",\n    \"mitigations\",\n    \"rollout_plan\",\n    \"long_term_fix\",\n    \"regression_test_plan\",\n    \"notes\"\n  ],\n  \"dataset_doc_uuid\": \"dsid_a3fdfc45905f46f3988ad13f55ecce93\"\n}",

document.title: Conditional multitenant rate limiter priority skew causing transient under-enforcement
document.content:
{
  "key": "ENG-428317",
  "team": "engineering",
  "title": "Conditional multitenant rate limiter priority skew causing transient under-enforcement",
  "status": "In Progress",
  "priority": "P1",
  "created_at": "2026-03-12",
  "updated_at": "2026-03-14",
  "creator": "Lina Chen",
  "assignee": "Marco Ruiz",
  "project": "RateEngine 2.0 - correctness",
  "cycle": "2026-Q1-Cycle 5",
  "estimate": "5",
  "due_date": "2026-03-21",
  "labels": [
    "billing",
    "rate-limiter",
    "investigation",
    "high-impact"
  ],
  "description": "Intermittent cases where per-key priority overrides combined with per-org and per-route policies result in transient under-enforcement (requests allowed when they should be throttled). Observed as short windows of elevated usage for a small set of tenants after shard reassignment and policy hot-reload. This ticket captures investigation, repro, short-term mitigation, and a long-term fix plan.",
  "reproduction_steps": [
    "1) Create two tenants T1 and T2 sharing a shard (sticky-shard assignment enabled).",
    "2) Configure per-org policy: default priority = low, per-route quota = 1000/min.",
    "3) Configure per-key override for a service key K1 belonging to T1: priority = high, burst credits = +200.",
    "4) Start a steady stream of requests from T1 at near-quota rate; verify enforcement hitting quota windows.",
    "5) Trigger a shard reassignment for one edge node (simulate instance bounce or maintenance) while simultaneously applying a policy hot-reload that changes route fallback behavior.",
    "6) Observe a ~10-30s window where requests for K1 are allowed beyond quota; metrics show credits attributed to the wrong in-memory bucket and enforcement checks returning allow from fast-path cache.",
    "7) Collect tracer spans and edge logs for the window; reproduce locally using the shard-reassignment harness and time-accelerated policy reloads."
  ],
  "impact": "Transient over-allow for small number of tenants leading to underbilling and potential customer perception issues; visible as short-lived bursts up to ~2x expected throughput for affected keys. Affects hosted and dedicated clusters during rolling updates or instance restarts.",
  "customer_impact": "medium",
  "logs_snapshot": [
    "edge: allow decision fastpath: key=K1 shard=sh-23 cache_hit=true priority=high quota_window_id=2026-03-12T10:04:00Z",
    "shard-reassign: lease=renewal failover->sh-27 old_owner=sh-23 new_owner=sh-27",
    "policy-hot-reload: version=v2026-03-12-1 route-fallback=enabled",
    "meter-commit: credits_applied target_bucket=org:T2:key:Kx unexpected=true amount=200"
  ],
  "hypothesis": "A race between sticky-shard mapping update and policy hot-reload causes fast-path cache entries (priority and credit pointers) to be re-keyed incorrectly. Per-key overrides store a pointer to a tenant-scoped credit bucket; during reassignment we are dereferencing a stale pointer and applying credits to the wrong tenant's bucket. Enforcement uses the fast-path decision if cache present, so the wrong credits cause an allow where a deny should occur.",
  "experiment_results": "Replayed the sequence in staging using the shard-reassign harness. With no policy reload the issue did not occur. When timed policy reload coincided with reassignment, we reproduced the over-allow consistently. Enabling stronger pointer validation (temporary patch) eliminated the over-allows in the harness.",
  "root_cause": "Sticky-shard pointer (in-memory bucket reference) is validated only by shard id but not by tenant id during fast-path credit application. Policy hot-reload mutates the route/priority indices while a shard transfer copies pointers; combined these can produce a transient pointer that points at an unrelated tenant's bucket. Enforcement fast-path accepts the cache without full tenant-level validation.",
  "mitigations": "Short-term patch deployed to staging: on fast-path cache hit, perform tenant-id validation on the cached credit pointer before applying credits. Also increased grace period on shard handoff to reduce overlap. Rolled patch to canary edge fleet.",
  "rollout_plan": "1) Canary for 2 hours on low-traffic region with added telemetry (done). 2) Gradual ramp to 30% of traffic with continued trace sampling for next 24 hours. 3) Full rollout after 48 hours if no regressions. 4) Follow with a database reconciliation backfill job to detect credits misapplied in last 7 days and create accounting fixes if needed.",
  "long_term_fix": "Refactor in-memory credit pointer representation to be immutable and namespaced by tenant+shard+route. Replace pointer dereference fast-path with a lightweight validation token check (versioned binder). Add unit and property tests for concurrent shard handoff + policy reload scenarios.",
  "regression_test_plan": "Add deterministic concurrency tests to runtime-policy-simulator: combinations of shard reassignment, policy hot-reload, per-key overrides, and burst credit application. Add e2e test in CI harness that exercises rolling updates with randomized interleavings. Add a smoke check after canary verifying no over-allow traces in last 10 minutes.",
  "dependencies": [
    "ENG-430001 (shard-handoff-stabilization)",
    "ENG-429112 (policy-hot-reload-atomicity)",
    "ENG-421007 (prefetch-credit-tombstone-investigation)"
  ],
  "links": [
    "https://confluence.redwood/inference/rateengine-2.0/priority-pointer-design",
    "https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving/pull/8523 (staging short-term patch)",
    "https://grafana.redwood/board/edge-allow-spikes?from=now-1d&org=tenant",
    "s3://redwood-logs/2026-03-12/shard-hand-off-traces.tar.gz"
  ],

# Cross-language streaming startup hang

## Symptom
A streaming call establishes transport but the consumer yields nothing at startup (or until close). Incidence varies by SDK/HTTP stack and TCP chunk boundaries.

## Diagnosis
The strongest reproduced signature is an SSE framing/parser boundary defect, not a runtime-wide startup failure: the first `data:` event is split inside JSON and the client parser waits indefinitely for a delimiter instead of carrying the incomplete event into the next chunk. Redwood Python 0.6.1 with httpx 0.24.3 reproduced this; 0.6.2 fixed accumulation across chunk boundaries. Cross-language parity guidance also shows inconsistent connect/first-byte and idle-timeout behavior across Python, TypeScript, and Go, so identical server bytes can present differently.

## Reproduction / validation
1. Capture raw bytes while streaming and force the first SSE JSON object to split at randomized offsets before the blank-line terminator.
2. Compare raw-byte progress with SDK iterator progress.
3. Validate that Python 0.6.1 stalls on the supplied split and 0.6.2 yields after the second fragment; run equivalent fixtures in TS and Go.
4. A rising server first-token latency without bytes is a different signature and does not validate this diagnosis.

## Reversible mitigation
Upgrade affected Python clients to 0.6.2. If upgrade is blocked, use `.stream_raw()` and accumulate complete SSE events; add bounded connect/first-byte and read-idle timeouts. Roll back the shim once upgraded. Do not blindly retry a partially consumed non-idempotent stream.

## Uncertainty
High confidence for the reproduced Python case. Medium confidence that every reported language is the same defect: TS/Go timeout differences may expose a server/proxy stall instead. Confirm with raw bytes and per-language versions before broad attribution.

## Evidence
- `/knowledge/company/sources/slack/support/1799003333-py-sdk-streaming-slow-first-byte-partial-prefix.json` (`dsid_bd52d657b63a4a4ba589e05e78182d9f`)
- `/knowledge/company/sources/confluence/eng-developer-experience/sdk-guides/sdk-parity-matrix-auth-retry-timeouts-streaming.json` (`dsid_bced6413bb6f414a882fb9cbaf8c7448`)

# Predictive autoscaling reacts late to known load

## Symptom
Capacity changes only near or after a known demand ramp, producing queue growth while the load was available in advance.

## Diagnosis
Treat this as a forecast-to-provisioning bridge problem. Scheduled profiles have a configurable pre-warm lead time (documented default 10 minutes); if that lead is shorter than GPU provisioning plus model/KV warmup, the system is predictively correct but operationally late. A consistent one-to-three-hour offset instead points to local-time schedules interpreted as UTC. If forecast timestamps are stale and scaling waits for queue depth, the predictor signal was rejected and the controller fell back to reactive behavior.

## Reproduction / validation
1. Compare scheduled event time/timezone, forecast timestamp and horizon, scale decision time, node-ready time, model-ready time, and demand onset.
2. Replay a scheduled profile with lead time below measured p95 time-to-ready, then with lead time above it plus safety margin.
3. Validate timezone by replaying the same explicit UTC instant.
4. Distinguish stale forecast fallback by verifying forecast age and queue-depth-triggered decisions.

## Reversible mitigation
Temporarily raise the minimum replica/capacity bound across the ramp window. Increase scheduled pre-warm lead time to measured p95 end-to-end readiness plus margin, and encode the schedule with an explicit timezone. Revert the higher floor after validation to avoid persistent overprovisioning.

## Uncertainty
The report does not include timestamps, so evidence supports three distinguishable causes rather than one proven cause. Lead-time insufficiency is the best fit for “known load, reacts late”; timezone offset or stale forecast must be ruled out from the timeline.

## Evidence
- `/knowledge/company/sources/github/pr-42812-scheduled-profiles-and-fairness-scaler.json` (`dsid_28d4ab23e7c74795ac809e8d9deef9ad`)
- `/knowledge/company/sources/confluence/customer-success-and-support/known-issues-and-workarounds/predictive-autoscaling-known-issues.json` (`dsid_07daff0e8966460f86c297b6939b607a`)

# Incorrect throttling during shard reassignment and policy reload

## Symptom
Transient allow/deny decisions are attributed to the wrong tenant when sticky-shard reassignment overlaps a policy hot reload, especially with per-key overrides or fallback-route toggles.

## Diagnosis
The authoritative RateEngine incident identifies a fast-path pointer validation race. Shard transfer copies an in-memory credit-bucket pointer while reload mutates route/priority indexes. The cache validates shard ID but not tenant ID, so a transient pointer can reference another tenant's bucket. Applying those credits causes incorrect enforcement (the captured case was over-allow).

## Reproduction / validation
Use the shard-reassign harness with per-key overrides and burst credits:
1. Reassignment alone: no error.
2. Policy reload alone: no error.
3. Time reload to overlap reassignment: repeatable over-allow.
4. Enable tenant-ID pointer validation: over-allows disappear.
Add randomized interleavings and verify no mismatched target-bucket trace.

## Reversible mitigation
On every fast-path hit, validate tenant ID on the cached credit pointer before applying credits; increase shard-handoff grace to reduce overlap. Canary with high trace sampling and roll back if latency or deny-rate regressions appear. Operationally, serialize reload and reassignment for affected pools until the immutable versioned binder ships.

## Uncertainty
High confidence in the overlap race and over-allow mechanism from deterministic staging validation. Broader “incorrect throttling” can include over-deny or metering drift; those require separate traces and should not be inferred from this evidence. Historical misapplied credits may require reconciliation.

## Evidence
- `/knowledge/company/sources/linear/engineering/ENG-428317-conditional-multitenant-ratelimiter-priority-skew.json` (`dsid_a3fdfc45905f46f3988ad13f55ecce93`)

              "text": "[Document context]\nTitle: Incident report: cross-language streaming startup hang\nSource: Aisha Bello SRE incident triage\nPath: /artifacts/incidents/cross-language-streaming-startup-hang.md\nWorkspace: task/aisha-streaming-startup-hang\n\n# Cross-language streaming startup hang\n\n## Symptom\nA streaming call establishes transport but the consumer yields nothing at startup (or until close). Incidence varies by SDK/HTTP stack and TCP chunk boundaries.\n\n## Diagnosis\nThe strongest reproduced signature is an SSE framing/parser boundary defect, not a runtime-wide startup failure: the first `data:` event is split inside JSON and the client parser waits indefinitely for a delimiter instead of carrying the incomplete event into the next chunk. Redwood Python 0.6.1 with httpx 0.24.3 reproduced this; 0.6.2 fixed accumulation across chunk boundaries. Cross-language parity guidance also shows inconsistent connect/first-byte and idle-timeout behavior across Python, TypeScript, and Go, so identical server bytes can present differently.\n\n## Reproduction / validation\n1. Capture raw bytes while streaming and force the first SSE JSON object to split at randomized offsets before the blank-line terminator.\n2. Compare raw-byte progress with SDK iterator progress.\n3. Validate that Python 0.6.1 stalls on the supplied split and 0.6.2 yields after the second fragment; run equivalent fixtures in TS and Go.\n4. A rising server first-token latency without bytes is a different signature and does not validate this diagnosis.\n\n## Reversible mitigation\nUpgrade affected Python clients to 0.6.2. If upgrade is blocked, use `.stream_raw()` and accumulate complete SSE events; add bounded connect/first-byte and read-idle timeouts. Roll back the shim once upgraded. Do not blindly retry a partially consumed non-idempotent stream.\n\n## Uncertainty\nHigh confidence for the reproduced Python case. # Cross-language streaming startup hang

## Symptom
A streaming call establishes transport but the consumer yields nothing at startup (or until close). Incidence varies by SDK/HTTP stack and TCP chunk boundaries.

## Diagnosis
The strongest reproduced signature is an SSE framing/parser boundary defect, not a runtime-wide startup failure: the first `data:` event is split inside JSON and the client parser waits indefinitely for a delimiter instead of carrying the incomplete event into the next chunk. Redwood Python 0.6.1 with httpx 0.24.3 reproduced this; 0.6.2 fixed accumulation across chunk boundaries. Cross-language parity guidance also shows inconsistent connect/first-byte and idle-timeout behavior across Python, TypeScript, and Go, so identical server bytes can present differently.

## Reproduction / validation
1. Capture raw bytes while streaming and force the first SSE JSON object to split at randomized offsets before the blank-line terminator.
2. Compare raw-byte progress with SDK iterator progress.
3. Validate that Python 0.6.1 stalls on the supplied split and 0.6.2 yields after the second fragment; run equivalent fixtures in TS and Go.
4. A rising server first-token latency without bytes is a different signature and does not validate this diagnosis.

## Reversible mitigation
Upgrade affected Python clients to 0.6.2. If upgrade is blocked, use `.stream_raw()` and accumulate complete SSE events; add bounded connect/first-byte and read-idle timeouts. Roll back the shim once upgraded. Do not blindly retry a partially consumed non-idempotent stream.

## Uncertainty
High confidence for the reproduced Python case. Medium confidence that every reported language is the same defect: TS/Go timeout differences may expose a server/proxy stall instead. Confirm with raw bytes and per-language versions before broad attribution.

A reproduced startup-like streaming hang occurred when the first SSE JSON event was split across network chunks and the client parser failed to carry the partial event forward. Redwood Python 0.6.2 fixed the reproduced 0.6.1 case; raw-byte capture is required before extending the diagnosis to TS or Go.

## Outcome

Diagnosis captured with reversible mitigation and validation criteria.

# Predictive autoscaling reacts late to known load

## Symptom
Capacity changes only near or after a known demand ramp, producing queue growth while the load was available in advance.

## Diagnosis
Treat this as a forecast-to-provisioning bridge problem. Scheduled profiles have a configurable pre-warm lead time (documented default 10 minutes); if that lead is shorter than GPU provisioning plus model/KV warmup, the system is predictively correct but operationally late. A consistent one-to-three-hour offset instead points to local-time schedules interpreted as UTC. If forecast timestamps are stale and scaling waits for queue depth, the predictor signal was rejected and the controller fell back to reactive behavior.

## Reproduction / validation
1. Compare scheduled event time/timezone, forecast timestamp and horizon, scale decision time, node-ready time, model-ready time, and demand onset.
2. Replay a scheduled profile with lead time below measured p95 time-to-ready, then with lead time above it plus safety margin.
3. Validate timezone by replaying the same explicit UTC instant.
4. Distinguish stale forecast fallback by verifying forecast age and queue-depth-triggered decisions.

## Reversible mitigation
Temporarily raise the minimum replica/capacity bound across the ramp window. Increase scheduled pre-warm lead time to measured p95 end-to-end readiness plus margin, and encode the schedule with an explicit timezone. Revert the higher floor after validation to avoid persistent overprovisioning.

## Uncertainty
The report does not include timestamps, so evidence supports three distinguishable causes rather than one proven cause. Lead-time insufficiency is the best fit for “known load, reacts late”; timezone offset or stale forecast must be ruled out from the timeline.

2. Replay a scheduled profile with lead time below measured p95 time-to-ready, then with lead time above it plus safety margin.
3. Validate timezone by replaying the same explicit UTC instant.
4. Distinguish stale forecast fallback by verifying forecast age and queue-depth-triggered decisions.

## Reversible mitigation
Temporarily raise the minimum replica/capacity bound across the ramp window. Increase scheduled pre-warm lead time to measured p95 end-to-end readiness plus margin, and encode the schedule with an explicit timezone. Revert the higher floor after validation to avoid persistent overprovisioning.

## Uncertainty
The report does not include timestamps, so evidence supports three distinguishable causes rather than one proven cause. Lead-time insufficiency is the best fit for “known load, reacts late”; timezone offset or stale forecast must be ruled out from the timeline.

              "text": "[Document context]\nTitle: Incident report: incorrect throttling during shard reassignment and policy reload\nSource: Aisha Bello SRE incident triage\nPath: /artifacts/incidents/shard-reassignment-policy-reload-throttling.md\nWorkspace: task/aisha-shard-policy-throttling\n\n# Incorrect throttling during shard reassignment and policy reload\n\n## Symptom\nTransient allow/deny decisions are attributed to the wrong tenant when sticky-shard reassignment overlaps a policy hot reload, especially with per-key overrides or fallback-route toggles.\n\n## Diagnosis\nThe authoritative RateEngine incident identifies a fast-path pointer validation race. # Incorrect throttling during shard reassignment and policy reload

## Symptom
Transient allow/deny decisions are attributed to the wrong tenant when sticky-shard reassignment overlaps a policy hot reload, especially with per-key overrides or fallback-route toggles.

## Diagnosis
The authoritative RateEngine incident identifies a fast-path pointer validation race. Shard transfer copies an in-memory credit-bucket pointer while reload mutates route/priority indexes. The cache validates shard ID but not tenant ID, so a transient pointer can reference another tenant's bucket. Applying those credits causes incorrect enforcement (the captured case was over-allow).

## Reproduction / validation
Use the shard-reassign harness with per-key overrides and burst credits:
1. Reassignment alone: no error.
2. Policy reload alone: no error.
3. Time reload to overlap reassignment: repeatable over-allow.
4. Enable tenant-ID pointer validation: over-allows disappear.
Add randomized interleavings and verify no mismatched target-bucket trace.

## Reversible mitigation
On every fast-path hit, validate tenant ID on the cached credit pointer before applying credits; increase shard-handoff grace to reduce overlap. Canary with high trace sampling and roll back if latency or deny-rate regressions appear. Operationally, serialize reload and reassignment for affected pools until the immutable versioned binder ships.

## Uncertainty
High confidence in the overlap race and over-allow mechanism from deterministic staging validation. Broader “incorrect throttling” can include over-deny or metering drift; those require separate traces and should not be inferred from this evidence. Historical misapplied credits may require reconciliation.

## Evidence
- `/knowledge/company/sources/linear/engineering/ENG-428317-conditional-multitenant-ratelimiter-priority-skew.json` (`dsid_a3fdfc45905f46f3988ad13f55ecce93`)

              "text": "[Document context]\nTitle: Incident report: cross-language streaming startup hang\nSource: Aisha Bello SRE incident triage\nPath: /artifacts/incidents/cross-language-streaming-startup-hang.md\nWorkspace: task/aisha-streaming-startup-hang\n\n# Cross-language streaming startup hang\n\n## Symptom\nA streaming call establishes transport but the consumer yields nothing at startup (or until close). Incidence varies by SDK/HTTP stack and TCP chunk boundaries.\n\n## Diagnosis\nThe strongest reproduced signature is an SSE framing/parser boundary defect, not a runtime-wide startup failure: the first `data:` event is split inside JSON and the client parser waits indefinitely for a delimiter instead of carrying the incomplete event into the next chunk. Redwood Python 0.6.1 with httpx 0.24.3 reproduced this; 0.6.2 fixed accumulation across chunk boundaries. Cross-language parity guidance also shows inconsistent connect/first-byte and idle-timeout behavior across Python, TypeScript, and Go, so identical server bytes can present differently.\n\n## Reproduction / validation\n1. Capture raw bytes while streaming and force the first SSE JSON object to split at randomized offsets before the blank-line terminator.\n2. Compare raw-byte progress with SDK iterator progress.\n3. Validate that Python 0.6.1 stalls on the supplied split and 0.6.2 yields after the second fragment; run equivalent fixtures in TS and Go.\n4. A rising server first-token latency without bytes is a different signature and does not validate this diagnosis.\n\n## Reversible mitigation\nUpgrade affected Python clients to 0.6.2. If upgrade is blocked, use `.stream_raw()` and accumulate complete SSE events; add bounded connect/first-byte and read-idle timeouts. Roll back the shim once upgraded. Do not blindly retry a partially consumed non-idempotent stream.\n\n## Uncertainty\nHigh confidence for the reproduced Python case. Medium confidence that every reported language is the same defect: TS/Go timeout differences may expose a server/proxy stall instead. Confirm with raw bytes and per-language versions before broad attribution.",

# Cross-language streaming startup hang

## Symptom
A streaming call establishes transport but the consumer yields nothing at startup (or until close). Incidence varies by SDK/HTTP stack and TCP chunk boundaries.

## Diagnosis
The strongest reproduced signature is an SSE framing/parser boundary defect, not a runtime-wide startup failure: the first `data:` event is split inside JSON and the client parser waits indefinitely for a delimiter instead of carrying the incomplete event into the next chunk. Redwood Python 0.6.1 with httpx 0.24.3 reproduced this; 0.6.2 fixed accumulation across chunk boundaries. Cross-language parity guidance also shows inconsistent connect/first-byte and idle-timeout behavior across Python, TypeScript, and Go, so identical server bytes can present differently.

## Reproduction / validation
1. Capture raw bytes while streaming and force the first SSE JSON object to split at randomized offsets before the blank-line terminator.
2. Compare raw-byte progress with SDK iterator progress.
3. Validate that Python 0.6.1 stalls on the supplied split and 0.6.2 yields after the second fragment; run equivalent fixtures in TS and Go.
4. A rising server first-token latency without bytes is a different signature and does not validate this diagnosis.

## Reversible mitigation
Upgrade affected Python clients to 0.6.2. If upgrade is blocked, use `.stream_raw()` and accumulate complete SSE events; add bounded connect/first-byte and read-idle timeouts. Roll back the shim once upgraded. Do not blindly retry a partially consumed non-idempotent stream.

## Uncertainty
High confidence for the reproduced Python case. Medium confidence that every reported language is the same defect: TS/Go timeout differences may expose a server/proxy stall instead. Confirm with raw bytes and per-language versions before broad attribution.

              "text": "[Document context]\nTitle: Incident report: predictive autoscaling reacts late to known load\nSource: Aisha Bello SRE incident triage\nPath: /artifacts/incidents/predictive-autoscaling-known-load-lag.md\nWorkspace: task/aisha-predictive-autoscaling-lag\n\n# Predictive autoscaling reacts late to known load\n\n## Symptom\nCapacity changes only near or after a known demand ramp, producing queue growth while the load was available in advance.\n\n## Diagnosis\nTreat this as a forecast-to-provisioning bridge problem. Scheduled profiles have a configurable pre-warm lead time (documented default 10 minutes); if that lead is shorter than GPU provisioning plus model/KV warmup, the system is predictively correct but operationally late. A consistent one-to-three-hour offset instead points to local-time schedules interpreted as UTC. If forecast timestamps are stale and scaling waits for queue depth, the predictor signal was rejected and the controller fell back to reactive behavior.\n\n## Reproduction / validation\n1. Compare scheduled event time/timezone, forecast timestamp and horizon, scale decision time, node-ready time, model-ready time, and demand onset.\n2. Replay a scheduled profile with lead time below measured p95 time-to-ready, then with lead time above it plus safety margin.\n3. Validate timezone by replaying the same explicit UTC instant.\n4. Distinguish stale forecast fallback by verifying forecast age and queue-depth-triggered decisions.\n\n## Reversible mitigation\nTemporarily raise the minimum replica/capacity bound across the ramp window. Increase scheduled pre-warm lead time to measured p95 end-to-end readiness plus margin, and encode the schedule with an explicit timezone. Revert the higher floor after validation to avoid persistent overprovisioning.\n\n## Uncertainty\nThe report does not include timestamps, so evidence supports three distinguishable causes rather than one proven cause. Lead-time insufficiency is the best fit for “known load, reacts late”; timezone offset or stale forecast must be ruled out from the timeline.",

# Predictive autoscaling reacts late to known load

## Symptom
Capacity changes only near or after a known demand ramp, producing queue growth while the load was available in advance.

## Diagnosis
Treat this as a forecast-to-provisioning bridge problem. Scheduled profiles have a configurable pre-warm lead time (documented default 10 minutes); if that lead is shorter than GPU provisioning plus model/KV warmup, the system is predictively correct but operationally late. A consistent one-to-three-hour offset instead points to local-time schedules interpreted as UTC. If forecast timestamps are stale and scaling waits for queue depth, the predictor signal was rejected and the controller fell back to reactive behavior.

## Reproduction / validation
1. Compare scheduled event time/timezone, forecast timestamp and horizon, scale decision time, node-ready time, model-ready time, and demand onset.
2. Replay a scheduled profile with lead time below measured p95 time-to-ready, then with lead time above it plus safety margin.
3. Validate timezone by replaying the same explicit UTC instant.
4. Distinguish stale forecast fallback by verifying forecast age and queue-depth-triggered decisions.

## Reversible mitigation
Temporarily raise the minimum replica/capacity bound across the ramp window. Increase scheduled pre-warm lead time to measured p95 end-to-end readiness plus margin, and encode the schedule with an explicit timezone. Revert the higher floor after validation to avoid persistent overprovisioning.

## Uncertainty
The report does not include timestamps, so evidence supports three distinguishable causes rather than one proven cause. Lead-time insufficiency is the best fit for “known load, reacts late”; timezone offset or stale forecast must be ruled out from the timeline.

              "text": "[Document context]\nTitle: Incident report: incorrect throttling during shard reassignment and policy reload\nSource: Aisha Bello SRE incident triage\nPath: /artifacts/incidents/shard-reassignment-policy-reload-throttling.md\nWorkspace: task/aisha-shard-policy-throttling\n\n# Incorrect throttling during shard reassignment and policy reload\n\n## Symptom\nTransient allow/deny decisions are attributed to the wrong tenant when sticky-shard reassignment overlaps a policy hot reload, especially with per-key overrides or fallback-route toggles.\n\n## Diagnosis\nThe authoritative RateEngine incident identifies a fast-path pointer validation race. Shard transfer copies an in-memory credit-bucket pointer while reload mutates route/priority indexes. The cache validates shard ID but not tenant ID, so a transient pointer can reference another tenant's bucket. Applying those credits causes incorrect enforcement (the captured case was over-allow).\n\n## Reproduction / validation\nUse the shard-reassign harness with per-key overrides and burst credits:\n1. Reassignment alone: no error.\n2. Policy reload alone: no error.\n3. Time reload to overlap reassignment: repeatable over-allow.\n4. Enable tenant-ID pointer validation: over-allows disappear.\nAdd randomized interleavings and verify no mismatched target-bucket trace.\n\n## Reversible mitigation\nOn every fast-path hit, validate tenant ID on the cached credit pointer before applying credits; increase shard-handoff grace to reduce overlap. Canary with high trace sampling and roll back if latency or deny-rate regressions appear. Operationally, serialize reload and reassignment for affected pools until the immutable versioned binder ships.\n\n## Uncertainty\nHigh confidence in the overlap race and over-allow mechanism from deterministic staging validation. Broader “incorrect throttling” can include over-deny or metering drift; those require separate traces and should not be inferred from this evidence. Historical misapplied credits may require reconciliation.\n\n## Evidence\n- `/knowledge/company/sources/linear/engineering/ENG-428317-conditional-multitenant-ratelimiter-priority-skew.json` (`dsid_a3fdfc45905f46f3988ad13f55ecce93`)",

# Incorrect throttling during shard reassignment and policy reload

## Symptom
Transient allow/deny decisions are attributed to the wrong tenant when sticky-shard reassignment overlaps a policy hot reload, especially with per-key overrides or fallback-route toggles.

## Diagnosis
The authoritative RateEngine incident identifies a fast-path pointer validation race. Shard transfer copies an in-memory credit-bucket pointer while reload mutates route/priority indexes. The cache validates shard ID but not tenant ID, so a transient pointer can reference another tenant's bucket. Applying those credits causes incorrect enforcement (the captured case was over-allow).

## Reproduction / validation
Use the shard-reassign harness with per-key overrides and burst credits:
1. Reassignment alone: no error.
2. Policy reload alone: no error.
3. Time reload to overlap reassignment: repeatable over-allow.
4. Enable tenant-ID pointer validation: over-allows disappear.
Add randomized interleavings and verify no mismatched target-bucket trace.

## Reversible mitigation
On every fast-path hit, validate tenant ID on the cached credit pointer before applying credits; increase shard-handoff grace to reduce overlap. Canary with high trace sampling and roll back if latency or deny-rate regressions appear. Operationally, serialize reload and reassignment for affected pools until the immutable versioned binder ships.

## Uncertainty
High confidence in the overlap race and over-allow mechanism from deterministic staging validation. Broader “incorrect throttling” can include over-deny or metering drift; those require separate traces and should not be inferred from this evidence. Historical misapplied credits may require reconciliation.

## Evidence
- `/knowledge/company/sources/linear/engineering/ENG-428317-conditional-multitenant-ratelimiter-priority-skew.json` (`dsid_a3fdfc45905f46f3988ad13f55ecce93`)

              "ordinal": 0,
              "text": "[Document context]\nTitle: Incident report: predictive autoscaling reacts late to known load\nSource: Aisha Bello SRE incident triage\nPath: /artifacts/incidents/predictive-autoscaling-known-load-lag.md\nWorkspace: task/aisha-predictive-autoscaling-lag\n\n# Predictive autoscaling reacts late to known load\n\n## Symptom\nCapacity changes only near or after a known demand ramp, producing queue growth while the load was available in advance.\n\n## Diagnosis\nTreat this as a forecast-to-provisioning bridge problem. Scheduled profiles have a configurable pre-warm lead time (documented default 10 minutes); if that lead is shorter than GPU provisioning plus model/KV warmup, the system is predictively correct but operationally late. A consistent one-to-three-hour offset instead points to local-time schedules interpreted as UTC. If forecast timestamps are stale and scaling waits for queue depth, the predictor signal was rejected and the controller fell back to reactive behavior.\n\n## Reproduction / validation\n1. Compare scheduled event time/timezone, forecast timestamp and horizon, scale decision time, node-ready time, model-ready time, and demand onset.\n2. Replay a scheduled profile with lead time below measured p95 time-to-ready, then with lead time above it plus safety margin.\n3. Validate timezone by replaying the same explicit UTC instant.\n4. Distinguish stale forecast fallback by verifying forecast age and queue-depth-triggered decisions.\n\n## Reversible mitigation\nTemporarily raise the minimum replica/capacity bound across the ramp window. Increase scheduled pre-warm lead time to measured p95 end-to-end readiness plus margin, and encode the schedule with an explicit timezone. Revert the higher floor after validation to avoid persistent overprovisioning.\n\n## Uncertainty\nThe report does not include timestamps, so evidence supports three distinguishable causes rather than one proven cause. Lead-time insufficiency is the best fit for “known load, reacts late”; timezone offset or stale forecast must be ruled out from the timeline.",

# Predictive autoscaling reacts late to known load

## Symptom
Capacity changes only near or after a known demand ramp, producing queue growth while the load was available in advance.

## Diagnosis
Treat this as a forecast-to-provisioning bridge problem. Scheduled profiles have a configurable pre-warm lead time (documented default 10 minutes); if that lead is shorter than GPU provisioning plus model/KV warmup, the system is predictively correct but operationally late. A consistent one-to-three-hour offset instead points to local-time schedules interpreted as UTC. If forecast timestamps are stale and scaling waits for queue depth, the predictor signal was rejected and the controller fell back to reactive behavior.

## Reproduction / validation
1. Compare scheduled event time/timezone, forecast timestamp and horizon, scale decision time, node-ready time, model-ready time, and demand onset.
2. Replay a scheduled profile with lead time below measured p95 time-to-ready, then with lead time above it plus safety margin.
3. Validate timezone by replaying the same explicit UTC instant.
4. Distinguish stale forecast fallback by verifying forecast age and queue-depth-triggered decisions.

## Reversible mitigation
Temporarily raise the minimum replica/capacity bound across the ramp window. Increase scheduled pre-warm lead time to measured p95 end-to-end readiness plus margin, and encode the schedule with an explicit timezone. Revert the higher floor after validation to avoid persistent overprovisioning.

## Uncertainty
The report does not include timestamps, so evidence supports three distinguishable causes rather than one proven cause. Lead-time insufficiency is the best fit for “known load, reacts late”; timezone offset or stale forecast must be ruled out from the timeline.

              "ordinal": 0,
              "text": "[Document context]\nTitle: Incident report: incorrect throttling during shard reassignment and policy reload\nSource: Aisha Bello SRE incident triage\nPath: /artifacts/incidents/shard-reassignment-policy-reload-throttling.md\nWorkspace: task/aisha-shard-policy-throttling\n\n# Incorrect throttling during shard reassignment and policy reload\n\n## Symptom\nTransient allow/deny decisions are attributed to the wrong tenant when sticky-shard reassignment overlaps a policy hot reload, especially with per-key overrides or fallback-route toggles.\n\n## Diagnosis\nThe authoritative RateEngine incident identifies a fast-path pointer validation race. Shard transfer copies an in-memory credit-bucket pointer while reload mutates route/priority indexes. The cache validates shard ID but not tenant ID, so a transient pointer can reference another tenant's bucket. Applying those credits causes incorrect enforcement (the captured case was over-allow).\n\n## Reproduction / validation\nUse the shard-reassign harness with per-key overrides and burst credits:\n1. Reassignment alone: no error.\n2. Policy reload alone: no error.\n3. Time reload to overlap reassignment: repeatable over-allow.\n4. Enable tenant-ID pointer validation: over-allows disappear.\nAdd randomized interleavings and verify no mismatched target-bucket trace.\n\n## Reversible mitigation\nOn every fast-path hit, validate tenant ID on the cached credit pointer before applying credits; increase shard-handoff grace to reduce overlap. Canary with high trace sampling and roll back if latency or deny-rate regressions appear. Operationally, serialize reload and reassignment for affected pools until the immutable versioned binder ships.\n\n## Uncertainty\nHigh confidence in the overlap race and over-allow mechanism from deterministic staging validation. Broader “incorrect throttling” can include over-deny or metering drift; those require separate traces and should not be inferred from this evidence. Historical misapplied credits may require reconciliation.\n\n## Evidence\n- `/knowledge/company/sources/linear/engineering/ENG-428317-conditional-multitenant-ratelimiter-priority-skew.json` (`dsid_a3fdfc45905f46f3988ad13f55ecce93`)",

# Incorrect throttling during shard reassignment and policy reload

## Symptom
Transient allow/deny decisions are attributed to the wrong tenant when sticky-shard reassignment overlaps a policy hot reload, especially with per-key overrides or fallback-route toggles.

## Diagnosis
The authoritative RateEngine incident identifies a fast-path pointer validation race. Shard transfer copies an in-memory credit-bucket pointer while reload mutates route/priority indexes. The cache validates shard ID but not tenant ID, so a transient pointer can reference another tenant's bucket. Applying those credits causes incorrect enforcement (the captured case was over-allow).

## Reproduction / validation
Use the shard-reassign harness with per-key overrides and burst credits:
1. Reassignment alone: no error.
2. Policy reload alone: no error.
3. Time reload to overlap reassignment: repeatable over-allow.
4. Enable tenant-ID pointer validation: over-allows disappear.
Add randomized interleavings and verify no mismatched target-bucket trace.

## Reversible mitigation
On every fast-path hit, validate tenant ID on the cached credit pointer before applying credits; increase shard-handoff grace to reduce overlap. Canary with high trace sampling and roll back if latency or deny-rate regressions appear. Operationally, serialize reload and reassignment for affected pools until the immutable versioned binder ships.

## Uncertainty
High confidence in the overlap race and over-allow mechanism from deterministic staging validation. Broader “incorrect throttling” can include over-deny or metering drift; those require separate traces and should not be inferred from this evidence. Historical misapplied credits may require reconciliation.

## Evidence
- `/knowledge/company/sources/linear/engineering/ENG-428317-conditional-multitenant-ratelimiter-priority-skew.json` (`dsid_a3fdfc45905f46f3988ad13f55ecce93`)

              "ordinal": 0,
              "text": "[Document context]\nTitle: Incident report: predictive autoscaling reacts late to known load\nSource: Aisha Bello SRE incident triage\nPath: /artifacts/incidents/predictive-autoscaling-known-load-lag.md\nWorkspace: task/aisha-predictive-autoscaling-lag\n\n# Predictive autoscaling reacts late to known load\n\n## Symptom\nCapacity changes only near or after a known demand ramp, producing queue growth while the load was available in advance.\n\n## Diagnosis\nTreat this as a forecast-to-provisioning bridge problem. Scheduled profiles have a configurable pre-warm lead time (documented default 10 minutes); if that lead is shorter than GPU provisioning plus model/KV warmup, the system is predictively correct but operationally late. A consistent one-to-three-hour offset instead points to local-time schedules interpreted as UTC. If forecast timestamps are stale and scaling waits for queue depth, the predictor signal was rejected and the controller fell back to reactive behavior.\n\n## Reproduction / validation\n1. Compare scheduled event time/timezone, forecast timestamp and horizon, scale decision time, node-ready time, model-ready time, and demand onset.\n2. Replay a scheduled profile with lead time below measured p95 time-to-ready, then with lead time above it plus safety margin.\n3. Validate timezone by replaying the same explicit UTC instant.\n4. Distinguish stale forecast fallback by verifying forecast age and queue-depth-triggered decisions.\n\n## Reversible mitigation\nTemporarily raise the minimum replica/capacity bound across the ramp window. Increase scheduled pre-warm lead time to measured p95 end-to-end readiness plus margin, and encode the schedule with an explicit timezone. Revert the higher floor after validation to avoid persistent overprovisioning.\n\n## Uncertainty\nThe report does not include timestamps, so evidence supports three distinguishable causes rather than one proven cause. Lead-time insufficiency is the best fit for “known load, reacts late”; timezone offset or stale forecast must be ruled out from the timeline.",

# Predictive autoscaling reacts late to known load

## Symptom
Capacity changes only near or after a known demand ramp, producing queue growth while the load was available in advance.

## Diagnosis
Treat this as a forecast-to-provisioning bridge problem. Scheduled profiles have a configurable pre-warm lead time (documented default 10 minutes); if that lead is shorter than GPU provisioning plus model/KV warmup, the system is predictively correct but operationally late. A consistent one-to-three-hour offset instead points to local-time schedules interpreted as UTC. If forecast timestamps are stale and scaling waits for queue depth, the predictor signal was rejected and the controller fell back to reactive behavior.

## Reproduction / validation
1. Compare scheduled event time/timezone, forecast timestamp and horizon, scale decision time, node-ready time, model-ready time, and demand onset.
2. Replay a scheduled profile with lead time below measured p95 time-to-ready, then with lead time above it plus safety margin.
3. Validate timezone by replaying the same explicit UTC instant.
4. Distinguish stale forecast fallback by verifying forecast age and queue-depth-triggered decisions.

## Reversible mitigation
Temporarily raise the minimum replica/capacity bound across the ramp window. Increase scheduled pre-warm lead time to measured p95 end-to-end readiness plus margin, and encode the schedule with an explicit timezone. Revert the higher floor after validation to avoid persistent overprovisioning.

## Uncertainty
The report does not include timestamps, so evidence supports three distinguishable causes rather than one proven cause. Lead-time insufficiency is the best fit for “known load, reacts late”; timezone offset or stale forecast must be ruled out from the timeline.

# Incorrect throttling during shard reassignment and policy reload

## Symptom
Transient allow/deny decisions are attributed to the wrong tenant when sticky-shard reassignment overlaps a policy hot reload, especially with per-key overrides or fallback-route toggles.

## Diagnosis
The authoritative RateEngine incident identifies a fast-path pointer validation race. Shard transfer copies an in-memory credit-bucket pointer while reload mutates route/priority indexes. The cache validates shard ID but not tenant ID, so a transient pointer can reference another tenant's bucket. Applying those credits causes incorrect enforcement (the captured case was over-allow).

## Reproduction / validation
Use the shard-reassign harness with per-key overrides and burst credits:
1. Reassignment alone: no error.
2. Policy reload alone: no error.
3. Time reload to overlap reassignment: repeatable over-allow.
4. Enable tenant-ID pointer validation: over-allows disappear.
Add randomized interleavings and verify no mismatched target-bucket trace.

## Reversible mitigation
On every fast-path hit, validate tenant ID on the cached credit pointer before applying credits; increase shard-handoff grace to reduce overlap. Canary with high trace sampling and roll back if latency or deny-rate regressions appear. Operationally, serialize reload and reassignment for affected pools until the immutable versioned binder ships.

## Uncertainty
High confidence in the overlap race and over-allow mechanism from deterministic staging validation. Broader “incorrect throttling” can include over-deny or metering drift; those require separate traces and should not be inferred from this evidence. Historical misapplied credits may require reconciliation.

Use the shard-reassign harness with per-key overrides and burst credits:
1. Reassignment alone: no error.
2. Policy reload alone: no error.
3. Time reload to overlap reassignment: repeatable over-allow.
4. Enable tenant-ID pointer validation: over-allows disappear.
Add randomized interleavings and verify no mismatched target-bucket trace.

## Reversible mitigation
On every fast-path hit, validate tenant ID on the cached credit pointer before applying credits; increase shard-handoff grace to reduce overlap. Canary with high trace sampling and roll back if latency or deny-rate regressions appear. Operationally, serialize reload and reassignment for affected pools until the immutable versioned binder ships.

## Uncertainty
High confidence in the overlap race and over-allow mechanism from deterministic staging validation. Broader “incorrect throttling” can include over-deny or metering drift; those require separate traces and should not be inferred from this evidence. Historical misapplied credits may require reconciliation.

## Evidence
- `/knowledge/company/sources/linear/engineering/ENG-428317-conditional-multitenant-ratelimiter-priority-skew.json` (`dsid_a3fdfc45905f46f3988ad13f55ecce93`)

Memory type: episodic_memory

Confidence: 0.96
Owner: Aisha Bello
Tags: rate-limiter, shard-handoff, policy-reload, race

## Summary

Deterministic staging tests showed that overlapping sticky-shard reassignment and policy hot reload could leave a fast-path credit pointer validated by shard but not tenant, applying credits to another tenant bucket. Tenant-ID validation eliminated the reproduced over-allows.

## Outcome

Diagnosis captured with reversible mitigation and validation criteria.

# Predictive autoscaling reacts late to known load

## Symptom
Capacity changes only near or after a known demand ramp, producing queue growth while the load was available in advance.

## Diagnosis
Treat this as a forecast-to-provisioning bridge problem. Scheduled profiles have a configurable pre-warm lead time (documented default 10 minutes); if that lead is shorter than GPU provisioning plus model/KV warmup, the system is predictively correct but operationally late. A consistent one-to-three-hour offset instead points to local-time schedules interpreted as UTC. If forecast timestamps are stale and scaling waits for queue depth, the predictor signal was rejected and the controller fell back to reactive behavior.

## Reproduction / validation
1. Compare scheduled event time/timezone, forecast timestamp and horizon, scale decision time, node-ready time, model-ready time, and demand onset.
2. Replay a scheduled profile with lead time below measured p95 time-to-ready, then with lead time above it plus safety margin.
3. Validate timezone by replaying the same explicit UTC instant.
4. Distinguish stale forecast fallback by verifying forecast age and queue-depth-triggered decisions.

## Reversible mitigation
Temporarily raise the minimum replica/capacity bound across the ramp window. Increase scheduled pre-warm lead time to measured p95 end-to-end readiness plus margin, and encode the schedule with an explicit timezone. Revert the higher floor after validation to avoid persistent overprovisioning.

## Uncertainty
The report does not include timestamps, so evidence supports three distinguishable causes rather than one proven cause. Lead-time insufficiency is the best fit for “known load, reacts late”; timezone offset or stale forecast must be ruled out from the timeline.

# Predictive autoscaling reacts late to known load

## Symptom
Capacity changes only near or after a known demand ramp, producing queue growth while the load was available in advance.

## Diagnosis
Treat this as a forecast-to-provisioning bridge problem. Scheduled profiles have a configurable pre-warm lead time (documented default 10 minutes); if that lead is shorter than GPU provisioning plus model/KV warmup, the system is predictively correct but operationally late. A consistent one-to-three-hour offset instead points to local-time schedules interpreted as UTC. If forecast timestamps are stale and scaling waits for queue depth, the predictor signal was rejected and the controller fell back to reactive behavior.

## Reproduction / validation
1. Compare scheduled event time/timezone, forecast timestamp and horizon, scale decision time, node-ready time, model-ready time, and demand onset.
2. Replay a scheduled profile with lead time below measured p95 time-to-ready, then with lead time above it plus safety margin.
3. Validate timezone by replaying the same explicit UTC instant.
4. Distinguish stale forecast fallback by verifying forecast age and queue-depth-triggered decisions.

## Reversible mitigation
Temporarily raise the minimum replica/capacity bound across the ramp window. Increase scheduled pre-warm lead time to measured p95 end-to-end readiness plus margin, and encode the schedule with an explicit timezone. Revert the higher floor after validation to avoid persistent overprovisioning.

## Uncertainty
The report does not include timestamps, so evidence supports three distinguishable causes rather than one proven cause. Lead-time insufficiency is the best fit for “known load, reacts late”; timezone offset or stale forecast must be ruled out from the timeline.

# Incorrect throttling during shard reassignment and policy reload

## Symptom
Transient allow/deny decisions are attributed to the wrong tenant when sticky-shard reassignment overlaps a policy hot reload, especially with per-key overrides or fallback-route toggles.

## Diagnosis
The authoritative RateEngine incident identifies a fast-path pointer validation race. Shard transfer copies an in-memory credit-bucket pointer while reload mutates route/priority indexes. The cache validates shard ID but not tenant ID, so a transient pointer can reference another tenant's bucket. Applying those credits causes incorrect enforcement (the captured case was over-allow).

## Reproduction / validation
Use the shard-reassign harness with per-key overrides and burst credits:
1. Reassignment alone: no error.
2. Policy reload alone: no error.
3. Time reload to overlap reassignment: repeatable over-allow.
4. Enable tenant-ID pointer validation: over-allows disappear.
Add randomized interleavings and verify no mismatched target-bucket trace.

## Reversible mitigation
On every fast-path hit, validate tenant ID on the cached credit pointer before applying credits; increase shard-handoff grace to reduce overlap. Canary with high trace sampling and roll back if latency or deny-rate regressions appear. Operationally, serialize reload and reassignment for affected pools until the immutable versioned binder ships.

## Uncertainty
High confidence in the overlap race and over-allow mechanism from deterministic staging validation. Broader “incorrect throttling” can include over-deny or metering drift; those require separate traces and should not be inferred from this evidence. Historical misapplied credits may require reconciliation.

## Evidence
- `/knowledge/company/sources/linear/engineering/ENG-428317-conditional-multitenant-ratelimiter-priority-skew.json` (`dsid_a3fdfc45905f46f3988ad13f55ecce93`)

# Runtime incident triage

Use this decision tree to distinguish three independent production signatures. Do not infer a shared root cause.

## Decision tree

1. **Is the primary symptom a stream that opens but yields no first event or stalls while raw transport remains open?**
   - **Yes:** Capture raw SSE bytes and SDK/HTTP versions.
     - Raw bytes advance, and the first JSON event is split before its event delimiter while the SDK iterator does not advance → **SSE first-fragment/parser signature**.
       - Validate with randomized chunk splits and a fixed SDK.
       - Mitigate by upgrading the affected SDK; otherwise use bounded raw-event accumulation plus connect/first-byte and read-idle timeouts.
     - No raw bytes before first token → investigate server scheduling/proxy buffering; this runbook does not establish the parser diagnosis.
     - Bytes stop mid-stream → classify idle timeout/disconnect separately.
   - **No:** continue.

2. **Does capacity arrive at or after a demand ramp that was forecast or scheduled in advance?**
   - **Yes:** Build one UTC timeline: schedule instant and timezone → forecast timestamp → scale decision → node ready → model/KV ready → traffic onset.
     - Decision is early but readiness is late, and pre-warm lead < p95 end-to-end readiness → **forecast-to-provision lead-time signature**.
     - Consistent 1–3 hour displacement → **timezone interpretation variant**.
     - Forecast is stale/unavailable and decisions begin only after queue growth → **stale-forecast reactive fallback variant**.
       - Mitigate reversibly with a temporary capacity floor, explicit timezone, and lead time set to p95 readiness plus margin.
   - **No:** continue.

3. **Do incorrect allow/deny decisions occur only when shard reassignment overlaps policy reload?**
   - **Yes:** Compare traces for tenant, shard, route, policy version, pointer/binder version, and target credit bucket.
     - Reassignment alone clean; reload alone clean; overlap reproduces; tenant-ID pointer validation removes errors → **RateEngine fast-path pointer race signature**.
       - Mitigate by tenant-validating cache hits, increasing handoff grace, or serializing reload and reassignment. Canary and watch latency/deny-rate.
       - Captured evidence proves over-allow; do not label over-deny or metering drift without separate traces.
   - **No:** none of these three packages is established; continue normal incident discovery.

## Evidence capture checklist

- Preserve timestamps in UTC, request/trace IDs, component versions, and raw inputs needed for deterministic replay.
- Prefer a negative control (each operation alone) and a positive overlap/split/short-lead case.
- Record mitigation rollback conditions.
- Keep evidence packages separate until each signature validates independently.

- `/artifacts/incidents/cross-language-streaming-startup-hang.md`
- `/artifacts/incidents/predictive-autoscaling-known-load-lag.md`
- `/artifacts/incidents/shard-reassignment-policy-reload-throttling.md`

arguments.summary: Decision procedure: raw SSE bytes versus iterator progress identifies parser-boundary hangs; schedule/forecast/decision/readiness UTC timelines identify lead-time, timezone, or stale-forecast autoscaling variants; negative controls plus overlap and tenant-pointer validation identify the shard-handoff/policy-reload RateEngine race. Keep the evidence packages independent.
arguments.outcome: Reviewed triage procedure consolidated from three published incident packages.

              "text": "[Document context]\nTitle: Runtime incident triage\nSource: Aisha Bello SRE reviewed incident packages\nPath: /knowledge/runbooks/runtime-incident-triage.md\nWorkspace: task/aisha-runtime-incident-triage-consolidation\n\n# Runtime incident triage\n\nUse this decision tree to distinguish three independent production signatures. Do not infer a shared root cause.\n\n## Decision tree\n\n1. **Is the primary symptom a stream that opens but yields no first event or stalls while raw transport remains open?**\n   - **Yes:** Capture raw SSE bytes and SDK/HTTP versions.\n     - Raw bytes advance, and the first JSON event is split before its event delimiter while the SDK iterator does not advance → **SSE first-fragment/parser signature**.\n       - Validate with randomized chunk splits and a fixed SDK.\n       - Mitigate by upgrading the affected SDK; otherwise use bounded raw-event accumulation plus connect/first-byte and read-idle timeouts.\n     - No raw bytes before first token → investigate server scheduling/proxy buffering; this runbook does not establish the parser diagnosis.\n     - Bytes stop mid-stream → classify idle timeout/disconnect separately.\n   - **No:** continue.\n\n2. **Does capacity arrive at or after a demand ramp that was forecast or scheduled in advance?**\n   - **Yes:** Build one UTC timeline: schedule instant and timezone → forecast timestamp → scale decision → node ready → model/KV ready → traffic onset.\n     - Decision is early but readiness is late, and pre-warm lead < p95 end-to-end readiness → **forecast-to-provision lead-time signature**.\n     - Consistent 1–3 hour displacement → **timezone interpretation variant**.\n     - Forecast is stale/unavailable and decisions begin only after queue growth → **stale-forecast reactive fallback variant**.\n       - Mitigate reversibly with a temporary capacity floor, explicit timezone, and lead time set to p95 readiness plus margin.\n   - **No:** continue.",

# Runtime incident triage

Use this decision tree to distinguish three independent production signatures. Do not infer a shared root cause.

## Decision tree

1. **Is the primary symptom a stream that opens but yields no first event or stalls while raw transport remains open?**
   - **Yes:** Capture raw SSE bytes and SDK/HTTP versions.
     - Raw bytes advance, and the first JSON event is split before its event delimiter while the SDK iterator does not advance → **SSE first-fragment/parser signature**.
       - Validate with randomized chunk splits and a fixed SDK.
       - Mitigate by upgrading the affected SDK; otherwise use bounded raw-event accumulation plus connect/first-byte and read-idle timeouts.
     - No raw bytes before first token → investigate server scheduling/proxy buffering; this runbook does not establish the parser diagnosis.
     - Bytes stop mid-stream → classify idle timeout/disconnect separately.
   - **No:** continue.

2. **Does capacity arrive at or after a demand ramp that was forecast or scheduled in advance?**
   - **Yes:** Build one UTC timeline: schedule instant and timezone → forecast timestamp → scale decision → node ready → model/KV ready → traffic onset.
     - Decision is early but readiness is late, and pre-warm lead < p95 end-to-end readiness → **forecast-to-provision lead-time signature**.
     - Consistent 1–3 hour displacement → **timezone interpretation variant**.
     - Forecast is stale/unavailable and decisions begin only after queue growth → **stale-forecast reactive fallback variant**.
       - Mitigate reversibly with a temporary capacity floor, explicit timezone, and lead time set to p95 readiness plus margin.
   - **No:** continue.

3. **Do incorrect allow/deny decisions occur only when shard reassignment overlaps policy reload?**

# Cross-language streaming startup hang

## Symptom
A streaming call establishes transport but the consumer yields nothing at startup (or until close). Incidence varies by SDK/HTTP stack and TCP chunk boundaries.

## Diagnosis
The strongest reproduced signature is an SSE framing/parser boundary defect, not a runtime-wide startup failure: the first `data:` event is split inside JSON and the client parser waits indefinitely for a delimiter instead of carrying the incomplete event into the next chunk. Redwood Python 0.6.1 with httpx 0.24.3 reproduced this; 0.6.2 fixed accumulation across chunk boundaries. Cross-language parity guidance also shows inconsistent connect/first-byte and idle-timeout behavior across Python, TypeScript, and Go, so identical server bytes can present differently.

## Reproduction / validation
1. Capture raw bytes while streaming and force the first SSE JSON object to split at randomized offsets before the blank-line terminator.
2. Compare raw-byte progress with SDK iterator progress.
3. Validate that Python 0.6.1 stalls on the supplied split and 0.6.2 yields after the second fragment; run equivalent fixtures in TS and Go.
4. A rising server first-token latency without bytes is a different signature and does not validate this diagnosis.

## Reversible mitigation
Upgrade affected Python clients to 0.6.2. If upgrade is blocked, use `.stream_raw()` and accumulate complete SSE events; add bounded connect/first-byte and read-idle timeouts. Roll back the shim once upgraded. Do not blindly retry a partially consumed non-idempotent stream.

## Uncertainty
High confidence for the reproduced Python case. Medium confidence that every reported language is the same defect: TS/Go timeout differences may expose a server/proxy stall instead. Confirm with raw bytes and per-language versions before broad attribution.",

# Predictive autoscaling reacts late to known load

## Symptom
Capacity changes only near or after a known demand ramp, producing queue growth while the load was available in advance.

## Diagnosis
Treat this as a forecast-to-provisioning bridge problem. Scheduled profiles have a configurable pre-warm lead time (documented default 10 minutes); if that lead is shorter than GPU provisioning plus model/KV warmup, the system is predictively correct but operationally late. A consistent one-to-three-hour offset instead points to local-time schedules interpreted as UTC. If forecast timestamps are stale and scaling waits for queue depth, the predictor signal was rejected and the controller fell back to reactive behavior.

3. Validate timezone by replaying the same explicit UTC instant.
